rationale: B wins because it spots the live wound in the facts: "Airtable is shipping agents that act on enterprise data — and won't say how often they get it right." That is sharper, more reportable, and more uncomfortable than A's safer trend wrapper, "The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market." A is disciplined, but B gives a founder the angle a real enterprise-AI reporter could interrogate today.
gaps_in_A: Misses the strongest angle in the update: agent reliability. The fact block explicitly says "agent-reliability data not disclosed," but A never turns that into a trust or governance story.
The category angle overclaims from one company: "The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market." That needs second evidence before it becomes a market story.
The competitive angle is real but soft: "that changes who it competes with" needs named categories of incumbents or buyer alternatives before it is more than positioning copy.
The refusal logic is too cautious. "Using absence as evidence" is bad for the valuation contrarian, but absence of reliability data is a legitimate hook when agents take actions on records.
gaps_in_B: The reliability angle slightly imports an outside premise: "2025-26's selling point for enterprise AI is autonomy." Plausible, but not in the update; support it or trim it.
The example "a bad draft sent" edges beyond the facts. The update says agents draft emails, not send them.
The counterposition angle says the category "already has incumbents" but names none. It correctly asks for that proof, but the angle is underpowered until the contrast exists.
The next step is a little out of order. `meanest-editor` is useful after a pitch draft exists; first, gather reliability proof and run journalist-fit-check on the chosen angle.
